headings: The original argument: validity and contested premises
What follows about access to moral status?
When moral immunity undermines moral praise
Two ten-question quizzes with answer keys
Two sets of fifteen discussion questions
intro: All six original prompts, the opening P1–P3 argument, and both response tracks are preserved. The replies and two original dialogues have been edited in place. Original curator note: A blackbox is a source of output for which the inner processes are unseen and unknown.
description: Can divine goodness be affirmed while all adverse evidence is excluded? The original argument, curator challenges, two dialogues, quizzes, and discussions.

replacements.1.1.0: The inference is valid on a consistent reading of its terms: the conclusion must follow if the three premises are true. That does not yet make the argument sound, which would require true premises as well. The main work is to explain what “cannot question” means and defend the links supplied by P1 and P2.
replacements.1.1.2: Assessment: P1 states a standard for justified moral authority: a claim to such authority must be open to meaningful assessment. This expresses the curator’s concern about immunity from scrutiny. It needs defense, however. Being forbidden to ask questions, being unable to understand every reason, and lacking any way to assess a claim are different conditions. A prohibition imposed by a community does not itself erase evidence someone already has.
replacements.1.1.4: Assessment: P2 supplies a further premise; it does not follow from P1. It is plausible if “question” means testing goodness against possible action-based counterevidence. It is too broad if it means any rational examination at all: one could still challenge a definition, an inference, or the reliability of a purported revelation. The argument must explain why those routes fail or restrict the conclusion to the action-based route.
replacements.1.1.6: Assessment: P3 can describe a believer’s rule for handling evidence, a definition of “Deity X,” or a claim that a necessarily good being cannot act badly. Those readings are not equivalent. Someone may say a cruel being would not qualify as God while still allowing cruelty to count against identifying a particular alleged speaker or actor as God. The curator’s target is clearest when every possible action of the very same alleged authority is protected from adverse assessment.
replacements.1.1.8: Assessment: The stated conclusion follows once the premises are accepted with those meanings held fixed. It concerns whether a person can rationally claim moral authority for X. It neither establishes that X is evil nor proves that X does not exist.
replacements.1.1.10: Let Q mean “we can meaningfully question X’s goodness,” A mean “we can rationally claim X is the legitimate moral arbiter,” and E mean “some imaginable action could count against X’s goodness.” P1 is ¬Q → ¬A.
replacements.1.1.11: P2 is ¬E → ¬Q, and P3 is ¬E. Applying P2 to P3 gives ¬Q.
replacements.1.1.12: Applying P1 to ¬Q gives ¬A. Each step uses the ordinary rule that if “if p then q” and p hold, q follows. The conclusion therefore follows without assuming that X actually performed a bad act.
replacements.1.1.13: Conclusion of Assessment: The argument validly exposes the cost of accepting all three premises. Its soundness requires defending P1 and P2 as well as establishing the relevant reading of P3. A useful test is whether the alleged evidence can distinguish a good authority from an authority whose conduct is excused regardless of what it does. Hidden motives alone do not settle that test.
replacements.1.2.0: The argument is valid if “cannot question” has one meaning throughout. Its soundness remains open because all three premises, not just P3, carry substantive commitments.
replacements.1.2.2: P1 connects rational authority with evaluability. An authority that forbids criticism may still be assessable from evidence; an authority whose goodness has been defined beyond all assessment presents a deeper problem. Use the second meaning if the argument is to address the curator’s moral black box.
replacements.1.2.4: P2 is contestable. A mathematical truth need not have an observational counterexample to be rationally examined; similarly, a defender could offer conceptual grounds for necessary goodness. Whether those grounds succeed and identify the relevant deity is a further question. Excluding action-based counterevidence therefore needs an additional argument before it excludes every form of inquiry.
replacements.1.2.6: P3 is best treated here as the immunity claim under examination, not an independently established fact about a deity. Ask its proponent whether apparently cruel conduct could undermine a claimed revelation, an interpretation, or the identity of the speaker. If so, some relevant assessment remains possible.
replacements.1.2.9: The deductive steps work: P3 together with P2 yields inability to question, and P1 yields inability rationally to claim authority. A critic can accept that structure while disputing a premise. Describing a premise as “logically sound” would obscure this difference between an inference’s form and a premise’s truth.
replacements.1.2.10: A defender might offer independent reasons for trusting X: an argument about necessary goodness, testimony, or a purported revelation. Those reasons must themselves be assessed. If their reliability is justified only by the goodness they are meant to establish, the defense risks circularity; if they are independent, the critic must address them rather than rule them out by definition.
replacements.1.2.11: The strongest application is conditional: if the defender excludes every adverse moral assessment while relying on comparable favorable assessments, ask what justifies the asymmetry. This preserves the force of the curator’s argument without declaring every belief in divine goodness irrational solely because it lacks a simple empirical falsifier.
replacements.2.1.0: Correct on a stronger interpretation of “no access,” but not as an unrestricted deduction from the original conclusion. The original argument denies a rational claim to X’s moral authority. To conclude that the person has no justified access to any aspect of X’s moral status requires further assumptions. The three premises give the following route:
replacements.2.1.4: Together, these premises yield the denial of a rational claim to X’s authority. If “no access” means no action-based procedure for distinguishing goodness from its absence, P2 and P3 support that narrower diagnosis. If it means no possible moral knowledge of X by any route, an additional premise must exclude independent grounds. The curator’s challenge remains: someone who rejects every adverse judgment as beyond human competence owes an explanation of how favorable judgments escape the same restriction.
replacements.2.2.0: The extension needs a qualification. Accepting P1–P3 commits someone to the stated conclusion about rationally claiming moral authority. It does not, by formal logic alone, yield the broader claim that they have no access whatsoever to X’s moral status.
replacements.2.2.4: On the action-based reading of P2, P3 blocks that way of testing goodness. It does not automatically rule out questioning the source’s identity, the concept of goodness, or an argument offered independently of actions.
replacements.2.2.6: The conclusion is therefore conditional on P1 and P2 as well as P3. A person who accepts only P3 can dispute the connecting premises; calling them logically forced to accept the conclusion without those premises would overstate the argument.
replacements.2.2.7: Nevertheless, “we cannot judge” cannot do selective work without explanation. If the same human capacities identify kindness as evidence for goodness but are disqualified whenever cruelty appears, the policy protects the conclusion rather than fairly assesses it. To claim broader moral access, the defender must specify a route that remains credible under their own restrictions.
replacements.3.1.0: The claim deserves scrutiny, especially when it is used to admit moral praise while excluding criticism. Its exact force depends on whether it expresses limited understanding or complete inability to assess divine goodness. Those positions have different consequences:
replacements.3.1.1: Implications for Rational Inquiry: Not understanding every reason for an action does not entail having no relevant evidence. A person may rationally remain uncertain. The stronger claim that no possible conduct could reduce confidence needs separate support; it should not be smuggled in through the uncontroversial fact that human knowledge is limited.
replacements.3.1.2: Tension with Premise 1: If the defender accepts P1 while denying every form of moral evaluation, the claim of rationally established authority conflicts with that premise. A defender who rejects P1 has a philosophical disagreement to answer, not an immediate formal contradiction. The issue is whether their alternative standard justifies authority rather than merely asserts it.
replacements.3.1.3: Issue of Moral Relevance: Even a clear command leaves two questions: did X issue it, and why should X’s instruction have moral authority? Complete opacity about goodness makes the second difficult to answer. Mere power or authorship does not, without another normative premise, establish a duty to obey.
replacements.3.1.4: Autonomy and Moral Agency: A person can delegate decisions for reasons they understand without grasping every detail. The problem is unconditional delegation that also disables checks on deception, misinterpretation, or harm. Ask what could count against the alleged authority or its spokesperson before surrendering those checks.
replacements.3.1.5: Logical Coherence: “We cannot fully understand X” and “we have some reason to trust X” can coexist. “We have no basis for any favorable or unfavorable assessment” conflicts with claiming an established favorable assessment on that same basis. The selective use of mystery must be exposed at that specific point.
replacements.3.1.6: The most precise criticism is thus of an evidential double standard. If suffering can never count against goodness because purposes are hidden, why does apparent beneficence count for it without equivalent scrutiny? A defender may propose an asymmetry, but must justify it. The mere possibility of a hidden good reason does not establish that such a reason exists in this case.
replacements.3.2.0: There is a serious tension when “God cannot be judged by humans” is used to block every unfavorable verdict while “God is morally good” remains a humanly justified assertion. The tension needs to be stated carefully rather than declared an inherent flaw in every theistic position.
replacements.3.2.1: A total ban on relevant adverse evidence resembles P3. A narrower admission that humans lack complete information does not. Treating these as interchangeable would make the criticism easier but less accurate.
replacements.3.2.2: If the defender accepts P1 and P2 as well as that total ban, the original conclusion follows. If they reject a connecting premise, the discussion must assess their reasons for doing so.
replacements.3.2.3: An illustrative comparison is a ruler whose kind acts count as evidence of goodness while every cruel act is excused by unknowable reasons. The comparison targets a rule for using evidence; it does not assume that a human ruler and a deity have identical knowledge, powers, or duties.
replacements.3.2.4: The double standard appears when the same kind of moral judgment is trusted in one direction and dismissed in the other without an independent reason. Calling that “having it both ways” is justified only after the difference in treatment has been shown, not merely because the defender mentions mystery.
replacements.3.2.5: Defining “good” as whatever X commands may avoid a contradiction, but it changes the question. It does not by itself explain why X’s commands deserve allegiance, why X exists, or why a particular message comes from X. Those claims still need reasons.
replacements.3.2.6: A successful defense must make its claimed grounds of moral trust intelligible enough to assess. The curator’s challenge is not a demand for omniscience; it is a demand that a declaration of goodness do more work than protecting an authority from every possible objection.
replacements.4.1.5: Alex: Suppose a leader’s kindness counts for him, but every cruel act is excused by secret reasons. What makes that assessment reliable? I am comparing the rule for evidence, not saying a deity has a leader’s limitations.
replacements.4.1.6: Theo: I would say my trust has another basis: revelation and an argument that God’s nature is necessarily good. It need not come only from judging individual actions.
replacements.4.1.7: Alex: Then those grounds matter. How do you identify a revelation as trustworthy without already assuming the speaker’s goodness? And what establishes that this particular claimed speaker has the nature your argument describes?
replacements.4.1.9: Alex: That states your proposed source of goodness. It does not yet justify our trust in this speaker. If the revelation is reliable because God is good, and we know God is good only because the revelation says so, the support runs in a circle.
replacements.4.1.11: Alex: If “divine logic” permits that circle to establish its own conclusion, how could we distinguish your speaker from a deceptive one making the same claim? Limited understanding can warrant caution, but it does not itself select the favorable interpretation.
replacements.4.1.13: Alex: Yes, but trust and a justification offered to someone else are different tasks. If there is independent support, we should examine it. If every adverse sign is disqualified and the only favorable support assumes the conclusion, the claim to moral authority has not been earned.
replacements.4.1.14: This dialogue preserves the curator’s challenge while allowing an independent-ground reply. The unresolved question is whether Theo can supply and defend those grounds without circularity or selectively disabling the standards used to assess them.
replacements.4.2.5: Nate: Does limited knowledge make every possible adverse judgment irrelevant, or does it make some judgments uncertain? Your conclusion needs the stronger claim, not merely the admission that we lack complete information.
replacements.4.2.7: Nate: A hidden justification may be possible, but that alone does not show it exists. If an apparent kindness supports goodness, why can apparent cruelty never count against it? What supports that difference?
replacements.4.2.9: Nate: Our argument says: if no action can count against goodness, and that prevents meaningful moral questioning, and such questioning is required to justify moral authority, then your claim to justified authority fails. You can dispute either connecting premise, but you need reasons beyond repeating the conclusion.
replacements.4.2.10: Tara: I accept that conditional argument, but I dispute the claim that action-based criticism is the only route to justification. I think God’s necessarily good nature provides another route. I would also question whether an apparently cruel command really came from God.
replacements.4.2.11: Nate: Then you have left the total black box: you allow assessment of the alleged source. We still need to examine your argument about divine nature and your reasons for identifying a message as divine. That is a live disagreement, not a reason to announce either that your case is proved or that all faith is irrational.
replacements.5.1.8: What problem does Alex identify in using revelation to establish goodness when the revelation’s reliability is itself justified only by that goodness?
replacements.5.1.10: What would Theo need to provide for his claim of independent grounds to advance the discussion?
replacements.5.1.11: Why does the dialogue distinguish personal trust from a justification offered to another person?
replacements.5.1.19: The support is circular: each claim is warranted only by assuming the other, with no independent support supplied.
replacements.5.1.21: Assessable reasons that do not rely only on the conclusion, including reasons to identify this alleged speaker as the good being described by the argument.
replacements.5.1.22: A personal commitment does not by itself supply another person with reasons to accept the authority. The claimed grounds must be stated and evaluated.
replacements.5.2.2: Which premise states the immunity claim under examination, and why should it not automatically be treated as an established fact about a deity?
replacements.5.2.3: What follows from accepting all three premises, and what stronger conclusion about moral access does not follow without additional support?
replacements.5.2.7: How does Tara respond to Nate’s conditional argument in the revised dialogue?
replacements.5.2.8: Why does Nate say Tara has left the total moral black box?
replacements.5.2.9: What still needs examination after Tara allows a purported divine command to be questioned?
replacements.5.2.13: P3. It can express a believer’s policy, a definition, or a modal claim about necessary goodness; these require different assessments.
replacements.5.2.14: One cannot rationally claim X as the legitimate moral arbiter. Total absence of justified access to any aspect of X’s moral status requires further assumptions.
replacements.5.2.15: Favorable assessment is treated as trustworthy while every comparable unfavorable assessment is disqualified, without an independent explanation for that asymmetry.
replacements.5.2.17: Nate gives the conditional P1–P3 inference and asks Tara to justify rejecting a connecting premise rather than treating the conclusion as self-evident.
replacements.5.2.18: She accepts the conditional structure but proposes independent grounds in divine nature and allows questions about the source of an allegedly cruel command.
replacements.5.2.19: She permits assessment of whether an alleged speaker or command is actually divine, rather than excluding every relevant adverse consideration.
replacements.5.2.20: Her argument about divine nature, its connection to this particular alleged source, and the reliability of the message still need assessment.
replacements.6.1.2: Can a deity be morally good even if humans cannot establish that goodness? How does the distinction between being good and being justified in claiming goodness affect this argument?
replacements.6.1.15: How far should P1’s requirement of meaningful critical assessment extend beyond this theological argument? Would every justified belief need an imaginable empirical falsifier?
replacements.6.2.9: Can you construct a clear hypothetical case in which favorable and unfavorable evidence are treated asymmetrically? What would establish that a real example follows the same pattern?

responseDecisions.1.1: Restored exact opening argument and premise/assessment progression. Gave explicit valid deduction; distinguished soundness, P2 independence, prohibition versus evaluability, and policy/definition/necessity readings of P3.
responseDecisions.1.2: Retained premise restatements and inference; corrected claim that only P3 needs support and that P2 is logically sound. Addressed independent grounds and circularity.
responseDecisions.2.1: Preserved curator follow-up verbatim and its three-premise recap. Qualified too-strong yes: original conclusion concerns rational authority; complete epistemic inaccessibility requires more.
responseDecisions.2.2: Retained P1–P3 quotations; separated action-based testing from other possible justification and exposed selective application of skepticism.
responseDecisions.3.1: Five-point list preserved. Distinguished limited understanding from total immunity, conditional inconsistency from disagreement, command identity from authority, and delegation from uncheckable obedience.
responseDecisions.3.2: Seven-paragraph progression preserved. Developed concrete ruler analogy with its limits, evidential asymmetry, definitional goodness and the remaining burden of justification.
responseDecisions.4.1: Retained Theo/Alex opening, faith and divine-logic turns, all thirteen speaker turns/order. Revised middle and end to test independent revelation, circularity and identity rather than infer all unfalsifiable beliefs irrational.
responseDecisions.4.2: Restored full eleven-turn Tara/Nate dialogue. Preserved alternation and initial stances; replaced forced capitulation with conditional argument, independent-ground reply and an explicit remaining disagreement.
responseDecisions.5.1: Ten questions/keys preserved. Revised three items and keys to match actual dialogue, manually checked remaining premise and authority answers.
responseDecisions.5.2: Ten questions/keys preserved. Corrected P3-as-fact, overbroad moral-access conclusion, and questions/keys tied to former forced capitulation.
responseDecisions.6.1: Fifteen questions retained; revised two to distinguish reality from justified belief and test scope of P1; thirteen retained verbatim.
responseDecisions.6.2: Fifteen questions retained; one revised to request a constructed case before assuming a real-world example; fourteen retained verbatim.

highlights: The conclusion follows from P1–P3 if the terms retain the same meanings; the premises still need defense.
Inability to see an agent’s motives differs from inability to assess any evidence of its goodness.
The curator’s challenge is sharpest when favorable evidence is admitted while all unfavorable evidence is excluded.
The argument challenges a justification of moral authority; it does not by itself prove that a deity is evil or nonexistent.
